scenes.tts: The number most often quoted for hair cells is forty microseconds. Is that how long one channel takes to open? It is not. It is a corrected delay, measured across a whole piece of tissue. Getting this right is the first step in reading any claim about transduction. So when someone says speed, which quantity did they measure?

scenes.tts: Corey and Hudspeth stimulated hair bundles in an in vitro bullfrog sacculus. They recorded the summed electrical response across the sheet of cells. The electrical time constant of the epithelium slows that signal. After correcting for it, the delay was forty microseconds, at twenty two degrees Celsius.

scenes.visual: A sheet of hair cells, bundles tilt; a summed trace is recorded across the sheet and rises slowly; the long recorded delay shrinks to the corrected 40 microseconds.

scenes.tts: Four different quantities travel under the word speed. A tissue latency is the delay of a population of cells. A channel time constant is how fast a current rises after a step. A molecular gain counts output events per input event. A behavioural latency runs from stimulus to movement, and no channel time constant stands in for it.
scenes.visual: Four cards in turn: tissue latency, channel time constant, molecular gain, behavioural latency, each with a small drawing.
scenes.narration: Four different quantities travel under the word speed. A tissue latency is the delay of a population of cells. A channel time constant is how fast a current rises after a step. scenes.tts: Now watch a channel time constant at work. Suppose a taste cell depolarizes for three milliseconds. In cultured mouse N two A cells, C A L H M one alone activated with a time constant above five hundred milliseconds. With C A L H M three added, the time constant was about ten milliseconds.
scenes.caption: Now watch a channel time constant at work. Suppose a taste cell depolarizes for 3 ms. In cultured mouse N2a cells, CALHM1 alone activated with a time constant above 500 ms. With CALHM3 added, the time constant was about 10 ms.
scenes.visual: A 3 ms depolarizing pulse; two channel rows on a membrane bar, CALHM1 alone and CALHM1 plus CALHM3, each tagged with its time constant.

scenes.tts: Model a channel that starts closed and rises as a single exponential. With a time constant of ten milliseconds, three milliseconds reaches about twenty six percent of the maximum. With five hundred, it reaches about point six percent, and the true fraction is smaller still. So the partner makes the channel about forty three times more responsive. These are teaching assumptions, not measured release.
scenes.caption: Model a channel that starts closed and rises as a single exponential. With a time constant of 10 ms, 3 ms reaches about 26% of the maximum. scenes.tts: A fast latency can fit a candidate channel. It is a constraint on the kinetics, not a proof. Speed alone does not identify the channel. The forty microseconds describes a tissue. The ten milliseconds describes a channel in cultured cells. Before you trust a speed, ask which quantity it is, and in which cell.
